intro: Few things derail a beach day faster than that familiar burning and constant urge to find a bathroom. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are one of the most common reasons travelers look for a doctor in Los Cabos — long flights, heat, less water than usual, swimsuits that stay wet for hours and a change in routine all add up.

The good news: a UTI is usually simple to check and treat when it is caught early. This guide covers the typical signs, what you can do while you arrange care, the warning signs that mean you should not wait, and how to see an English-speaking doctor at your hotel, villa or yacht in Cabo San Lucas, the Tourist Corridor or San José del Cabo.

p: Most UTIs on vacation are bladder infections (sometimes called cystitis). Typical signs include:
list: Burning or stinging when you urinate
A strong, frequent urge to go, often passing only small amounts
Feeling that the bladder never fully empties
Cloudy, dark or strong-smelling urine
Pink, red or brownish urine (a sign of blood)
Pressure or cramping in the lower belly
p_after: Some of these symptoms can also come from dehydration, irritation from swimwear or soaps, a vaginal infection, a sexually transmitted infection or a kidney stone. That is why an exam — and often a quick urine test — is the best way to know what is going on and get the right treatment.

sections.h2: Why UTIs are so common on a Cabo vacation
list: Heat and dehydration: sun, alcohol and long days outside mean you urinate less, giving bacteria more time to grow.
Holding it: boat trips, tours, golf rounds and long transfers make it easy to wait too long between bathroom breaks.
Wet swimsuits: sitting for hours in a damp suit by the pool or on a boat can irritate the area.
Travel days: flights and airport time often mean less water and fewer bathroom stops.
Honeymoons and romantic getaways: more frequent sex is a well-known trigger for bladder infections.

sections.h2: What you can do while you arrange care
p: These general steps can help you feel more comfortable while you contact a doctor. They are not a replacement for treatment:
list: Drink water steadily through the day, and use bottled or purified water.
Go when you feel the urge — do not hold it.
Cut back on alcohol, coffee and very sugary or fizzy drinks, which can irritate the bladder.
Change out of wet swimsuits soon after swimming and choose breathable cotton underwear.

Ask before taking anything. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before using pain relievers or over-the-counter urinary products, especially if you are pregnant, have kidney problems or take other medication.
p_after: Most bladder infections need prescription treatment, and in Mexico antibiotics are sold with a prescription. Taking leftover pills from home or guessing at a medication can mask symptoms or lead to the wrong treatment. A short visit gets you the right prescription the same day.

sections.h2: When a UTI needs urgent attention
p: Contact a doctor the same day — do not wait until you fly home — if you have any of these:
list: Fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, or shaking chills
Pain in your back or side, just below the ribs
Nausea or vomiting
Visible blood in the urine
Symptoms during pregnancy
UTI symptoms in a man, a child or an older adult
Diabetes, kidney disease, a weakened immune system or a urinary catheter
Symptoms that are not improving, or are getting worse, after starting treatment
p_after: Fever, back pain and vomiting together can mean the infection has reached the kidneys, which needs prompt medical care. Call 911 right away if you or someone with you has confusion, very fast breathing or heartbeat, fainting, a very high fever with severe weakness, or is unable to keep any fluids down — these can be signs of a serious infection that needs emergency care.

sections.h2: Seeing a doctor in Cabo without leaving your room

p: An English-speaking doctor comes to your hotel, villa or yacht 24/7, reviews your symptoms and history, examines you and prescribes treatment if appropriate. Typical arrival is 30–45 minutes in Cabo San Lucas and the Tourist Corridor, and up to about 60 minutes in San José del Cabo, Pedregal and Palmilla. Book a house-call doctor.
Staying near downtown Cabo San Lucas? You can be seen at our clinic on Francisco I. Madero, Centro, for $99 USD.
Whatever the doctor prescribes, plus bottled water or electrolytes, can be delivered to your room 24/7 — free over $50 USD (a fee may apply between 10 PM and 7 AM). Order pharmacy delivery.

p_after: There is no payment before the visit, and you receive an itemized invoice in English and USD to submit to your travel insurance (US and Canadian insurance accepted, subject to verification). All rates are on our prices page.

sections.h2: What to have ready for the doctor
p: A few details help the visit go quickly and make treatment safer:
list: When symptoms started and whether they are getting better or worse
Any fever, back pain, nausea or blood in the urine
Whether you are or could be pregnant
Medications you take, including birth control, and any drug allergies
Past UTIs and what treatment worked (or did not)
Your travel dates, so the doctor can plan around your flight home

sections.h2: How to lower your risk for the rest of the trip
list: Keep a refillable bottle of purified water with you and sip through the day.
Alternate alcoholic drinks with water, especially in the sun.
Take bathroom breaks before boat trips, tours and long drives.
Change out of wet swimsuits instead of lounging in them for hours.
Urinate soon after sex.
Finish any treatment exactly as prescribed, even once you feel better.
p_after: Dehydration plays a big role in many vacation illnesses. If the heat has you feeling drained, our guide on what to do if you get sick in Cabo covers the most common problems travelers face and how to get help fast.

faq.q: Can I get UTI antibiotics without a prescription in Cabo?
faq.a: In Mexico, antibiotics are sold with a prescription. A doctor visit at your hotel ($189 USD) or our clinic ($99 USD) lets you get the right prescription quickly, and we can deliver it to your room.

faq.q: How fast can a doctor see me for a UTI in Cabo San Lucas?
faq.a: Our English-speaking doctors are available 24/7. Typical arrival is 30 to 45 minutes in Cabo San Lucas and the Tourist Corridor, and up to about 60 minutes in San José del Cabo, Pedregal and Palmilla.

faq.q: Will my travel insurance cover a UTI visit in Cabo?
faq.a: Many travel insurance plans reimburse doctor visits abroad. You pay after the visit and receive an itemized invoice in English and USD to submit to your insurer. We accept international health and travel insurance from the United States and Canada, subject to policy verification and coverage confirmation.

faq.q: Is it safe to fly home with a UTI?
faq.a: Many people fly comfortably once treatment has started, but fever, back pain or vomiting should be checked by a doctor before you travel. Mention your flight time during the visit so the doctor can advise you.

faq.q: When is a UTI an emergency?
faq.a: Call 911 for confusion, fainting, very fast breathing or heartbeat, a very high fever with severe weakness, or if you cannot keep fluids down. Fever with back pain and vomiting needs a doctor the same day.
